newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour government gets into full swing.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour government gets into full swing.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government gets into full swing on Wednesday when parliament reconvenes to elect a new speaker and Foreign Minister Robin Cook meets his French and German counterparts.

Less than a week after their landslide victory and a day after new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown surprised financial markets with a quarter point rise in interest rates and by giving the Bank of England control over future rates, Cook set off on his first foreign trip to Paris and Bonn.

He is expected to keep up Labour's momentum by emphasising Britain's interest in promoting constructive engagement in the European Union during meetings with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette in Paris and Klaus Kinkel in Bonn.

"We want to take Britain out of a position of isolationism, out of inward-looking chauvinism and into being a leading member of an international community," he said in an interview shortly after his appointment.
Cook, promising a fresh start in foreign policy, has already said Britain will sign the Social Chapter on worker's rights and intends to focus on human rights and the environment.

Back in London, Prime Minister Tony Blair, fresh from his 44th birthday celebrations on Tuesday, will address the parliamentary Labour party. Later the new 659-member parliament with a record number of women will meet to elect a speaker.

Blair, who manoeuvred his party to the centre to secure its 179 seat majority, is expected to run a tight ship, telling the 418 Labour MPs that they won as New Labour and must govern as New Labour. The party divisions that dogged the Conservatives and contributed to their downfall will not be tolerated.
"The prime minister does not believe that because you did the right things in opposition you should suddenly stop in government," a Labour insider told The Times newspaper.
Meanwhile the Conservatives, still reeling from their disastrous defeat, were searching for a new leader after former prime minister John Major announced he was standing down last week.
The battle for the party leadership had just started but already recriminations were flying as candidates seeking the top job announced their intention.

Former interior minister Michael Howard and Eurosceptic John Redwood, who had unsuccessfully challenged Major for the leadership two years ago, announced they were in the running, as had ex finance minister Kenneth Clarke and right winger Peter Lilley.
Outgoing Welsh secretary William Hague, who at 36 will be the youngest contender, is expected to throw his hat in the ring on Wednesday.
Hague, after agreeing to a pact during a late night meeting with Howard which would have secured him the deputy leader's job if Howard won, backed out of the deal on Tuesday.
"It was a dream ticket," an aide to Howard said. "What is clear is that Mr Howard, when he went to bed, thought the deal was done."
Hague, already tipped to be a favourite, was playing his cards close to his chest, refusing to reveal what his plans are.
"I intend to make an announcement about what I intend to do tomorrow morning," he said on Tuesday.
Outgoing Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell is also expected to join the race.
